topics.title: Complex Numbers
topics.notes:
A complex number is z = a + bi, where i² = −1. Add and subtract by combining real and imaginary parts separately. To multiply, expand like brackets and replace i² with −1: (2 + 5i)(8 − 2i) = 16 + 36i + 10 = 26 + 36i. The most common error is forgetting that the −10i² term becomes +10.

The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi. Two facts follow: z − z̄ = 2bi (twice the imaginary part), and z·z̄ = a² + b², a real number. To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator so the denominator becomes real.

Polar form is z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), where r = √(a² + b²) is the modulus and θ is the argument. Always decide the quadrant first from the signs of a and b: 1 − i√3 is in the fourth quadrant, so θ = −60° = 300° = 5π/3. Using the calculator's tan⁻¹ alone gives the wrong quadrant for second- and third-quadrant numbers.

The logarithm of a complex number is multi-valued: log z = ln r + i(θ + 2πn) for any integer n. If a quadratic has a negative discriminant, it has no real roots, only a conjugate pair of complex roots.

KEY FORMULA: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), with r = √(a² + b²), and log z = ln r + i(θ + 2πn).
topics.keyFormula: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ)

topics.title: Sequences, Series & Induction
topics.notes:
An arithmetic progression (AP) adds the same difference each time: Uₙ = a + (n − 1)d. A geometric progression (GP) multiplies by the same ratio: Uₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹. Identify which one you have first. For 3, 5, 7, 9 the difference is 2, so Uₙ = 2n + 1. For 8, 2, 1/2 the ratio is 1/4, so Uₙ = 8(1/4)ⁿ⁻¹ = 2⁵⁻²ⁿ.

If you are given the sum Sₙ, the nth term is Uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁. Word problems about yearly increases (salary, falling bodies) are APs: the 10th term is a + 9d, not a + 10d.

The p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converges when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1. Useful sums to know: Σ r = n(n + 1)/2 and Σ r² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.

Mathematical induction has three steps: show the result for n = 1; assume it for n = k; then prove it for n = k + 1. You never assume the result for n = k + 1, since that is what you must prove. In the inductive step for a sum, add the (k + 1)th term to the formula for k and simplify to the formula with n = k + 1.

To expand a function like eˢⁱⁿˣ, substitute the series for sin x into the series for eᵘ and collect powers of x, checking that terms cancel (the x³ term vanishes).

KEY FORMULA: Uₙ = a + (n − 1)d (AP), Uₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹ (GP), and Uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.

topics.title: Quadratics, Roots & Inequalities
topics.notes:
For ax² + bx + c = 0, the sum of the roots is −b/a and the product is c/a. Most exam questions ask you to build a new equation from transformed roots: find the sum S and product P of the new roots from α + β and αβ, then write x² − Sx + P = 0 and clear fractions. For roots α² and β², use α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ. Always double-check by testing the signs: if the old equation has −5/2 as a product, a careless sign gives a wrong equation.

The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you the nature of the roots: positive gives two real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. The turning point of y = ax² + bx + c is at x = −b/2a, and it is a maximum when a < 0 and a minimum when a > 0.

For inequalities, factorise and use the sign of the parabola. If (x + 7)(x − 4) > 0, the answer is outside the roots (x < −7 or x > 4); if it is < 0, the answer lies between them. An absolute-value inequality |u| < c means −c < u < c. For a logarithm inequality such as log₃(…) < 3, remember to convert it to the argument being less than 3³ = 27, and that the argument must also be positive.

KEY FORMULA: Sum of roots = −b/a, product of roots = c/a, new equation x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0.

topics.title: Partial Fractions
topics.notes:
Partial fractions split one rational expression into simpler ones. First check that the numerator has a lower degree than the denominator; if not, divide first. Then match the factors of the denominator: a linear factor (x − a) gives A/(x − a); a repeated factor (x − a)² gives A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²; an irreducible quadratic (x² + c) gives (Bx + C)/(x² + c), and if it is repeated you need a term for each power.

The cover-up method is the fastest for distinct linear factors: to find the constant over (x − a), cover that factor and substitute x = a into what remains. For (8x − 17)/((x + 1)(x − 4)), at x = −1 you get (−25)/(−5) = 5, and at x = 4 you get 15/5 = 3. For a repeated factor, use cover-up for the highest power, then compare coefficients (for example the x² terms) to find the rest.

Always check your answer by substituting a simple value such as x = 0 into both sides. Also watch for cancellation: in (x⁴ + x)/(x(x² + 1)²) the numerator contains a factor x, which cancels, so the A/x term works out to zero even though the general form includes it.

KEY FORMULA: For distinct linear factors, A = (value of the rest of the fraction at x = a), e.g. (cover-up method).

topics.title: Trigonometric Identities
topics.notes:
Learn these identities well, because nearly every question is one of them. Double angle: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ, cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ, tan 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 − tan²θ). Compound angle: cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B. Sum-to-product: sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2) and sin A − sin B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) sin((A − B)/2). Shifts: tan(x + π/2) = −cot x.

For questions given one ratio, draw a right-angled triangle. If sin x = 3/5 then cos x = 4/5, tan x = 3/4, cot x = 4/3, csc x = 5/3 and sec x = 5/4. If tan x = 3/5 the hypotenuse is √34. The sign of the other ratios depends on the quadrant: for two obtuse angles, both cosines are negative, which changes the sign of cos A cos B.

To express tan 4θ, apply the double-angle formula twice. To express cos³x in multiple angles, use cos 3x = 4cos³x − 3cos x and rearrange: cos³x = (cos 3x + 3 cos x)/4. Another useful trick: 1 − cos²x = sin²x, so (1 − cos²x)csc²x = 1.

Work carefully with the order in a difference: sin 4θ − sin 6θ gives 2 cos 5θ sin(−θ) = −2 sin θ cos 5θ, with the minus sign.

KEY FORMULA: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.
topics.keyFormula: cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B

topics.title: Sets & Venn Diagrams
topics.notes:
A set is a collection of distinct elements. The union A ∪ B contains everything in A or B; the intersection A ∩ B contains only what is in both; the complement A′ contains every element of the universal set that is not in A. Work through brackets one step at a time: for (S ∩ T) ∪ R, find S ∩ T first.

The smallest universal set for two sets is their union. The power set of a set with n elements has 2ⁿ elements, so 5 elements give 32 and 6 give 64.

For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). For three sets: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C). Use this to find the number in all three. If a question says everyone studies at least one subject, the union equals the total. A probability question is then the count divided by the total number of pupils. Percentages: convert to counts first (60% of 400 is 240) and then use the two-set formula.

A sanity check is vital: if solving gives a negative number of people (as a faulty set of numbers can), the question is inconsistent and needs different data.

KEY FORMULA: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B), and a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.
topics.keyFormula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

topics.title: Binary Operations & Number Systems
topics.notes:
A binary operation takes two elements and combines them by a rule, written for example a ∘ b = a + b + ab/2. Evaluate it by substituting the values exactly, one pair at a time. For (2 ∘ 3) ∘ 4, first find 2 ∘ 3 = 8, then 8 ∘ 4 = 28. Do not rearrange the order unless you have proved the operation is associative.

To solve an equation involving an operation, substitute and solve as usual: if x * y = x² − y² − y and 3 * M = 7, then 9 − M² − M = 7, so M = 1 or −2. The answer must belong to the set the operation is defined on; if x must be an integer and your solution is 2/3, there is no solution.

An operation is commutative if swapping the elements gives the same result (a * b = b * a), and associative if (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). To test, swap and simplify: (p − q)²/(p + q) is commutative because (q − p)² = (p − q)², while (p − q)/(pq) is not because swapping changes its sign. De Morgan's laws belong to sets and logic, not to properties of binary operations.

Number systems: ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ ⊂ ℂ. Rational numbers are the only one of the common sets closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division (excluding zero).

KEY FORMULA: Commutative: a * b = b * a. Associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c).

topics.title: Permutations & Combinations
topics.notes:
Use a permutation when order matters and a combination when it does not. ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)! counts ordered selections of r from n, and ⁿCᵣ = n!/((n − r)! r!) counts unordered ones. Note that ⁿPₙ = n!, and that ⁿPᵣ is just the product of r descending factors starting at n: ¹⁰P₄ = 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040. To find (n, r) from a product, n is the largest factor and r is the number of factors.

For arrangements of the letters of a word, divide by the factorial of each repeated letter's count: CALCULUS has 8 letters with C, L and U each twice, so 8!/(2!2!2!). A word with all different letters, like PENCIL, has 6! arrangements.

For committees with separate groups, multiply the combinations for each group: 3 boys from 5 and 4 girls from 6 gives ⁵C₃ × ⁶C₄ = 10 × 15 = 150.

Binomial expansion: (a + b)ⁿ has general term ⁿCₖ aⁿ⁻ᵏ bᵏ. To find a particular term, work out the power of x in terms of k, set it equal to the power you want, and solve for k. For (2x² − 1/x)¹² the power of x is 24 − 3k, so x⁹ needs k = 5, giving ¹²C₅ × 2⁷ × (−1)⁵ = −101,376. Keep track of the signs and of the numerical factor from every part of the bracket.

KEY FORMULA: ⁿCᵣ = n!/((n − r)! r!) and the general binomial term is ⁿCₖ aⁿ⁻ᵏ bᵏ.
